Periods where the card is silent, from Lewis & Short: aedificātor late (the literal “builder” only in Vulg. Isa. 58.12; classically figurative, Cic. N.D. 1.9, or “fond of building”, Nep. Att. 13, Juv. 14.86); caementārius modern in Traupman’s sense (in Lewis & Short a mason, Jerome and the Vulgate); antīcum modern (Lewis & Short has only the adjective antīcus); ōstium antīcum post-classical (Morgan–Owens: Smith citing Festus); plumbārius classical (Vitruvius’s artificēs plumbāriī; the noun alone is in the Digest); diaeta as a suite of rooms classical (Lewis & Short’s “post-Augustan” is Pliny and Suetonius); laterum strūctor modern (Traupman pp. 162, 165); summum tabulātum, cella subterrānea, aedificium adstrūctum and pars domūs nova, veterī adstrūcta ours.

Where entry-149 and entry-174 give no source line for a word, the record cites Lewis & Short without a link: builder (s.v. aedificator), bricklayer (s.v. structor), rung (s.v. gradus). Added Traupman 329 to ferrum trānsversum (the card names Traupman without a page; checked in the text).

Recommended forms to check: īnsulātiō leads insulation, though the card calls the descriptions preferable in narration (mūnīmentum adversus frīgus is an alternative; parietēs adversus frīgus mūnīre heads insulate); extollō leads build up, with exstruō for the past tense as the card says; cumulus leads pile, as the card recommends, over the heading’s acervus; pertica leads scaffold pole over fistula; the descriptions lead base plate (lāmina sub fistulā posita) and coupler (vinculum quō duae fistulae conjunguntur), with lāmina and vinculum as alternatives.

Readers: the Libellus VII dialogue is cited formally, with “after Traupman’s colloquium on p. 162” moved into its English; the Cato, Agr. 14, 1 quotation (lintel) is cited to Cato, with “quoted in Libellus VII” in its English, because check_libelli rejects any other source that names a Libellus. Malleum habeō! sits in contractor (Theo playing the contractor) for want of a hammer record.

Splits to look at: compāgēs in scaffold (modern, Morgan–Owens) and framework (classical); caementum in rubble (classical) and cement (Traupman 288); fastīgium in gable and slope; tabulātum in storey and scaffold platform; diaeta in wing (ancient) and apartment (Traupman); dirt split into earth and grime; tabula from entries 150, 152 and 174 in board and insulation board; sōlārium from entries 195 and 426 in terrace; jānua and rēctum ōstium (entry-157) also as front-door alternatives. Avoid terms: concrētum and sessōrium, each with a note citing its ruling (concrete, sitting-room), and āla and calculus, as their cards say.

scripts/build.py derives the grammar of -eī genitives (pluteī, horreī, hypogēī, subtēgulāneī) as fifth declension; those terms set grammar explicitly, as do terms without a genitive (statūmen, pontēs, sessōrium, concrētum, calculus, āla, xystus, reserāre) and the plural pedeplāna.

Likely overlaps with cards converted in parallel (headwords may clash on merge): stone (sermo entry-27), build and dismantle / take apart (sermo entry-32), dig (domus entry-266, ludi entry-181), sand (ludi entry-180), wood (culina entry-128), slope (natura entry-199, entry-278), storeroom (culina entry-248), garage (vectura entry-536), storey (vectura entry-222, floor), furniture (domus entry-265), craftsman (urbs entry-544), ladder and rung (domus entry-88), scaffold pole (officina entry-161, pipe / tube), iron tools (officina entry-97), built-in wardrobe (domus entry-87). lime and plaster carry senses (for building; on walls) because natura (lime tree, lime fruit) and corpus (sticking plaster) use the same headwords.
